miniPosts.summary: Berlin Pride 2026 (CSD) holds its main parade on July 25. A local guide to the route, the whole Pride week, where to watch, and the history that makes Berlin a queer capital.

miniPosts.title: The Hidden Courtyards of Berlin: A Walk Through the Höfe Around Hackescher Markt
miniPosts.summary: Behind the facades around Hackescher Markt, Berlin hides a second layer: connected inner courtyards, the Höfe, that most visitors walk straight past. Here is which passages to step into and in what order, from the tiled Hackesche Höfe to a street-art courtyard, a rose garden and a hand-made candy workshop, all within a ten-minute walk.
miniPosts.alt: The illuminated Art Nouveau tiled facade of the first courtyard of the Hackesche Höfe in Berlin at night.

miniPosts.title: Telling Time in German: Why Halb Acht Is 7:30 and How Berlin Says the Rest
miniPosts.summary: Somebody says halb acht, you arrive at half past eight, and the table is gone. Berlin runs two clocks at once: everything written uses 24 hours, and almost everything spoken drops back to twelve and then counts towards the hour that has not arrived yet. Here is the one shift that makes German time make sense, the eastern viertel and dreiviertel forms you will hear around Berlin, the day codes on a museum door, and a dial you can turn to test all of it.
miniPosts.alt: The Urania World Clock on Alexanderplatz in Berlin, its metal cylinder marked with world cities above a lit band of hour numbers running past 12, 13, 14 and 15.

miniPosts.title: The Oberbaumbrücke: Berlin's Prettiest Bridge and the Border That Ran Through It
miniPosts.summary: It looks medieval, but it is younger than the U-Bahn, and for twenty-eight years the East-West border ran across the water beneath its arches. Here is the story of the Oberbaumbrücke and how to walk it.
miniPosts.alt: The Oberbaumbrücke carrying a U-Bahn over the Spree between Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain

posts.title: The Reichstag, Before and After: How One Building Holds Germany’s Whole Century
posts.summary: From the front the Reichstag looks like one stern old parliament with a modern glass hat. It is actually the most rebuilt, refought-over building in Germany: imperial showpiece, burnt-out shell, 1945 battlefield, Cold War dead end, and finally a working democracy. Here is the building before and after, the traces you can still find on the stone, and how to get inside the dome for free.
posts.alt: The Reichstag in Berlin at sunset, its stone facade lit warm gold beneath the modern glass dome, with the German flag flying.

posts.summary: Is Berlin walkable? The central sights are far closer than the map suggests, and flat underfoot. Here is how far apart they really are, the one walk to do on foot, and when to take the train instead.
